passages.happening:
“Solomon, however, took thirteen years to complete the construction of his entire palace” (verse 1). The chapter describes its buildings. The House of the Forest of Lebanon is a hundred cubits long, fifty wide and thirty high, with four rows of cedar pillars, cedar beams, and windows in three tiers (verses 2-5). There is a colonnade with a porch (verse 6), and ‘the Hall of Justice, where he was to judge’ (verse 7). Solomon's own house stands farther back, and he builds a house like it for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had married (verse 8).

All of it is built of costly stone, cut to size and trimmed with saws, on foundations of great stones some ten and some eight cubits long, with cedar beams above, and a great courtyard walled with dressed stone and cedar (verses 9-12).
passages.hearers:
Where this account sits is telling. It comes between the finishing of the temple's shell and the making of its furnishings, and it opens with a contrast: the temple took seven years, the palace thirteen. Some readers hear no criticism, since the palace was a larger group of buildings and David had prepared for the temple. Others hear the narrator raising an eyebrow at a king whose own house outgrew God's. The text does not settle it.

The House of the Forest of Lebanon, named for its rows of cedar pillars, was about 150 feet long and 75 feet wide, larger than the temple. The book later says Solomon kept gold shields there (10:17), and Isaiah mentions weapons stored in it, so it may have served as a hall and an armory. The Hall of Justice was the throne room where the king heard cases.

Palaces in that world were centers of government as well as royal homes, with throne rooms, halls, storerooms and private rooms. Cedar pillars and dressed stone were marks of great wealth. Setting the palace next to the temple also said something: the king ruled under God and near his house. The separate house for Pharaoh's daughter shows the rank of an Egyptian royal marriage.
passages.later: Isaiah remembers the hall as an armory in a time of danger: ‘On that day you looked to the weapons in the House of the Forest’ (Isaiah 22:8).
passages.asks: Solomon gave thirteen years to his own house and seven to God's. Ask what the time you give to your own comfort says beside the time you give to God's work. And ask whether a place for justice, like Solomon's hall, has room among the things you build.

passages.t: Huram, two pillars, and the Sea
passages.happening:
Solomon sends to Tyre for Huram, ‘the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali’, whose father was a man of Tyre and a worker in bronze. Huram has ‘great skill, understanding, and knowledge for every kind of bronze work’ (verse 14), and he does all Solomon's bronze work.

He casts two bronze pillars, each eighteen cubits high, with capitals five cubits high, decorated with network, chains, rows of pomegranates and the shape of lilies (verses 15-20). He sets them up at the porch of the temple. “The pillar to the south he named Jachin, and the pillar to the north he named Boaz” (verse 21).

He makes the Sea of cast metal, ‘measuring ten cubits from rim to rim, five cubits in height, and thirty cubits in circumference’ (verse 23). It stands on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each direction, and its rim is ‘fashioned like the brim of a cup, like a lily blossom’ (verse 26). It holds two thousand baths.
passages.hearers:
Huram, also spelled Hiram, is not King Hiram. He is described with the same three Hebrew words, for wisdom, understanding and knowledge, that Exodus uses for Bezalel, the craftsman of the tabernacle, which ties the temple to the tabernacle. In the Bible, skilled work in bronze, wood and stone is a form of wisdom and a gift that can serve God. Chronicles says that Huram's mother was from the tribe of Dan. Interpreters suggest she was of Danite descent and lived in Naphtali, or that the two books keep two traditions.

Freestanding pillars at a temple's entrance are known from other sites in the region. Their names are usually taken to mean he establishes (Jachin) and in him is strength (Boaz), though scholars differ on the exact sense. If Jachin means that God establishes, it may have announced that he upholds both the temple and David's line. Boaz is also the name of David's ancestor in Ruth; some scholars have wondered whether the pillar recalled him, but the text does not say so.

The Sea was a great basin about fifteen feet across. Ancient peoples often pictured the sea as chaos, and Canaanite stories told of the storm god defeating Yam, the sea. In the LORD's court the sea is a tamed vessel of water for washing, standing on oxen, perhaps a picture of his rule over every power. The twelve oxen facing the four directions may suggest Israel's twelve tribes, or the whole land. Pomegranates and lilies, signs of fruitfulness and life, repeat the garden of chapter 6.
passages.later: Exodus describes Bezalel with the same words: “And I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Chronicles adds what the Sea was for: ‘the priests used the Sea for washing’ (2 Chronicles 4:6).
passages.hard:
Does verse 23 get the measurement wrong, making pi equal to three?

The Sea is said to be ten cubits across and thirty around, which would make the ratio exactly three rather than about 3.14. Several reasonable answers are given. The numbers are rounded figures in an ancient building description, not an engineer's specification. Verse 26 says the rim was a handbreadth thick and flared like a cup, so the ten cubits may measure across the outer lip while the thirty cubits measure around the body below it; with a thick, flared rim, both measurements could be accurate.

Ancient builders used practical measures, and the text reports what was measured, not a lesson in geometry. Most readers conclude that the verse raises no real problem for the text's truthfulness.
passages.asks: A widow's son from Naphtali was given the skill to make the pillars of God's house. Ask what skill of your hands could serve God as truly as any prayer. And ask what you lean on, when the ground shifts, as Jachin and Boaz announced: God who establishes, and strength found in him.

passages.t: Stands, basins, and the gold furnishings
passages.happening:
Huram also makes ten bronze stands on wheels, each four cubits square and three high, their panels engraved with lions, oxen, cherubim and palm trees, each carrying a bronze basin that holds forty baths (verses 27-38). Five stand on the south side of the temple and five on the north, with the Sea at the southeast corner (verse 39). He makes the pots, shovels and sprinkling bowls, and the list sums up his work (verses 40-45). It is all cast in clay in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan (verse 46), and there is so much that ‘The weight of the bronze could not be determined’ (verse 47).

Solomon also makes the gold furnishings for inside the house: the golden altar, the golden table for the Bread of the Presence, ten lampstands of pure gold, five on each side before the inner room, and the basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, ladles and censers, with gold hinges for the doors (verses 48-50).

“So all the work that King Solomon had performed for the house of the LORD was completed” (verse 51). He brings in the silver, the gold and the furnishings his father David had dedicated, and puts them in the treasuries of the house.
passages.hearers:
The stands carried basins for washing the offerings. The detail of this chapter, almost tiring to read, is typical of building accounts in the Bible, like the tabernacle chapters at the end of Exodus. It shows that every part of God's house was made with care.

The work moves from bronze outside to gold inside. The closer one came to the presence of God, the more precious everything became, and washing basins stood in the court: coming near to God required cleansing.

The Jordan valley between Succoth and Zarethan had clay suited to casting large bronze objects, and casting on this scale needed molds and a skilled workforce.

None of this bronze lasted. King Ahaz later took the Sea off its oxen, and the Babylonians broke up the pillars, the stands and the Sea and carried the bronze away when they destroyed the temple. The first readers of Kings knew it.
passages.later:
The tabernacle had one lampstand: ‘Then you are to make a lampstand of pure, hammered gold’ (Exodus 25:31). Solomon's house had ten.

When Babylon took Jerusalem, “the Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars and stands and the bronze Sea in the house of the LORD, and they carried the bronze to Babylon” (2 Kings 25:13), as Jeremiah also records (Jeremiah 52:17).
passages.asks: Everything was made with care, down to the shovels and the hinges. Ask whether you give care to the small, unseen parts of your work for God. And ask what you would still have of God if, like Israel, you lost the bronze and the gold.
